title: API Performance, Capacity, and Traffic Engineering
centralQuestion: Where do time and capacity go, what is the first limiting resource, and which measured change improves the system without weakening correctness?
responsibility: Measure, model, and control latency, throughput, resource use, fairness, and overload behavior with comparable evidence.
incomingBoundary: The Course 4 observable and recoverable API 1.2 service with Security and Reliability Profiles 1.0 and migrations 001–008.
outgoingBoundary: Performance Profile 1.0, migration 009, workload identities, benchmark evidence, HTTP and query optimizations, concurrency and cache policy, traffic controls, capacity models, and performance release gates.
versionState: API 1.2, Security Profile 1.0, and Reliability Profile 1.0 preserved; Performance Profile 1.0 introduced; migrations 001–009.
languageStrategy: one primary implementation track plus one comparative reference track

modules.title: Measurement Contract and Critical Workloads
modules.centralQuestion: What exactly is being measured, under which workload and environment identity, and which correctness oracle still applies?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Freeze six critical workloads, measurement envelopes, outcome populations, evidence classes, and comparable baselines.
learningOutcomes: distinguish performance requirements from reliability objectives and capacity claims
derive critical workloads from inherited user journeys instead of endpoint popularity
choose an open, closed, or mixed load model deliberately
define offered, admitted, completed, rejected, and failed populations
hash identity-bearing workload and environment fields deterministically
write correctness oracles that survive optimization
reject an incomparable baseline before calculating improvement

modules.title: Benchmark Design and Statistical Interpretation
modules.centralQuestion: How do open and closed demand, warmup, sample size, missing outcomes, variation, and statistical uncertainty change benchmark meaning?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Build reproducible benchmark profiles, repeated runs, quantile and interval summaries, and accepted/rejected/inconclusive comparisons.
learningOutcomes: distinguish load generation, timing, outcome collection, and analysis
design open and closed schedules and explain their different questions
detect coordinated omission using intended start times
choose warmup and measurement windows from observed behavior
calculate nearest-rank quantiles and explain alternative algorithms
separate run-to-run variability from within-run latency distribution
use bootstrap intervals over independent run summaries cautiously
declare regression thresholds before seeing candidate results

modules.title: HTTP Efficiency and Representation Cost
modules.centralQuestion: Where do HTTP connections, representations, compression, conditional requests, range delivery, and streaming consume time and bytes?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Optimize artifact and metadata delivery while preserving authorization, ETags, ranges, and bounded memory.
learningOutcomes: separate resource state, selected representation, and transferred message
measure bytes and buffering alongside latency
apply strong and weak entity tags intentionally
evaluate conditional requests in the correct precedence
implement single byte-range requests and documented unsatisfied ranges
stream large bodies with bounded memory
choose compression from media type, size, CPU, and cache-key consequences
design authorization-aware cache directives and `Vary` behavior
reject optimizations that break checksums, ranges, or tenant isolation

modules.title: PostgreSQL Query and Persistence Performance
modules.centralQuestion: Which query plan, index, lock, pool, or pagination behavior is the first persistence bottleneck for a declared workload?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Capture before/after plans, add evidence-backed indexes, size database connections, and preserve owner-aware query semantics.
learningOutcomes: separate client wait, pool wait, lock wait, planning, execution, and transfer
read PostgreSQL text and JSON plans from the root downward
compare estimated and actual row counts
interpret sequential scans, index scans, bitmap scans, sorts, joins, and loops
design composite index column order from equality, range, and ordering predicates
preserve authorization and stable keyset pagination
measure read gain alongside write amplification and index size
size connection pools against database capacity rather than request concurrency
use `pg_stat_statements` as aggregate evidence without losing workload identity
write a reversible migration and a plan-regression gate

modules.title: Runtime Profiling and Allocation Control
modules.centralQuestion: Which Python or Node.js runtime phase consumes wall time, CPU, allocations, event-loop capacity, or serialization effort?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Profile named phases, detect blocking work, bound profiling overhead, and prove mechanism-level improvements.
learningOutcomes: separate wall-clock, process CPU, and allocation measurements
choose sampling, deterministic, or tracing profilers for the question
read call counts, cumulative time, self time, and caller relationships
use `tracemalloc` snapshots to locate Python allocation growth
measure Node event-loop delay and utilization
identify synchronous blocking inside asynchronous request paths
measure serialization and validation cost without bypassing them
avoid micro-optimizations that increase copying or memory
compare runtime-specific improvements through the shared workload envelope

modules.title: Queueing, Concurrency, and Backpressure
modules.centralQuestion: How do arrival rate, service time, queue depth, concurrency, fairness, and backpressure determine overload behavior?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Implement bounded admission, per-operation limits, queue accounting, permit release, and recovery after pressure.
learningOutcomes: identify every implicit and explicit queue in a request journey
apply Little’s Law with compatible populations and intervals
distinguish service time, waiting time, response time, and service demand
explain why tail latency rises rapidly near saturation
size concurrency from a limiting resource rather than CPU count folklore
bound queue length and waiting time
propagate cancellation without undoing committed work
design backpressure across API, worker, storage, and outbound stages
preserve fairness and avoid starvation
separate admission rejection from internal failure

modules.title: Caching, Freshness, and Invalidation
modules.centralQuestion: Which data is safe to cache, for whom, for how long, and who owns invalidation after mutation or failure?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Build authorization-aware keys, TTL/capacity policy, source-version invalidation, single-flight fills, and failure semantics.
learningOutcomes: distinguish HTTP, process-local, shared application, database, and client caches
classify values by mutability and authorization sensitivity
define complete cache keys and value envelopes
choose freshness and stale behavior explicitly
implement invalidation from durable change rather than best-effort route code
prevent cross-tenant and cross-policy reuse
bound entries, bytes, and concurrent fills
control cache stampedes and failure amplification
measure hit, miss, fill, stale, eviction, and origin cost
reject caches that improve latency while worsening correctness or tail load

modules.title: Traffic Shaping, Quotas, and Load Shedding
modules.centralQuestion: How should quotas, priorities, cost budgets, and load shedding preserve fairness and truthful 429/503 outcomes?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Implement multi-dimensional fixed-point budgets, tenant isolation, staged shedding, and rollback of partial reservations.
learningOutcomes: distinguish rate limits, quotas, concurrency limits, and capacity admission
choose dimensions that reflect resource cost
implement deterministic token-bucket arithmetic
bind policy to principal, tenant, operation, and service class
preserve fairness under skewed traffic
calculate truthful retry guidance
define a load-shedding ladder before overload
protect admitted work and critical control operations
measure offered, admitted, rejected, and completed traffic by reason
state local versus distributed enforcement limitations

modules.title: Capacity Modeling and Scaling Decisions
modules.centralQuestion: What capacity does the current system have, what uncertainty surrounds it, and which resource becomes the first bottleneck as demand grows?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Model CPU, connections, workers, queues, storage, egress, cost, headroom, and scaling decisions.
learningOutcomes: translate workload forecasts into resource demand
calculate service demand from utilization and throughput
identify the first bottleneck across CPU, database, memory, storage, network, and worker capacity
apply headroom and failure/maintenance assumptions
model queue drain and recovery capacity
represent uncertainty with ranges and scenarios
compare vertical, horizontal, optimization, and demand-shaping options
include stateful dependency and connection limits
estimate cost per useful completed unit
define trigger metrics and remeasurement conditions

modules.title: Performance Regression and Release Engineering
modules.centralQuestion: How does a performance change become a reproducible release decision rather than a favorable chart?
modules.capstoneIncrement: Build correctness-first regression gates, environment comparability, accepted/rejected/inconclusive candidates, and a performance dossier.
learningOutcomes: design a tiered performance verification pipeline
enforce identity and correctness before metric comparison
combine absolute and relative regression thresholds
handle noise through run series and inconclusive decisions
select stable mechanism-level CI tests
avoid brittle wall-clock gates on uncontrolled runners
write release acceptance, rollback, and remeasurement criteria
connect performance alerts and capacity triggers to operations
produce a reviewable performance dossier
sanitize and manifest the next-course handoff
